No power of $a$ has been cancelled. F.70 puts $a^{ck}$ in the ideal of the $c\times c$ minors of $F$. Reduction at a prime of the nonzero ring $B$ shows $c\le n+t$. For every $e\ge\max(L,ck,1)$, multiply the minor coefficients by $a^{e-ck}$ to obtain D.3s1, together with the already established D.3s2. When $c=0$, the minor ideal is $A$ and the same conclusion uses the empty determinant $1$. This proves (e) over arbitrary rings, including zero divisors. ∎

Proof of (f). Put $B=A_a$. If $B=0$, some power $a^L$ is zero. The zero differential module has the empty basis, and, as in (e), every $a^e$ with $e\ge\max(L,1)$ is elementary using $c=0$ and the empty minor $1$. Assume $B\ne0$.

First suppose $B$ is smooth and $\mathrm db_1,\ldots,\mathrm db_d$ is a basis with $b_i\in A$. Choose finite algebra generators $z_1,\ldots,z_n$ of $A$ over $R$ and the surjection $$P=R[X_1,\ldots,X_n,Y_1,\ldots,Y_d]\longrightarrow A, \qquad X_i\longmapsto z_i,\quad Y_j\longmapsto b_j.$$ Its kernel $J$ is finitely generated by F.44. The smoothness definition F.6, the presentation description of the naive cotangent complex F.11, and localization F.65 give the exact sequence $$0\longrightarrow M=(J/J^2)_a\xrightarrow{\mathrm d} B^n\oplus B^d\longrightarrow\Omega_{B/R}\longrightarrow0.$$ Here the two summands have coordinates $\mathrm dX_i$ and $\mathrm dY_j$. The map from the second summand to $\Omega_{B/R}$ is an isomorphism, because its images are the chosen basis. Consequently projection onto the first summand restricts to an isomorphism $M\to B^n$: for each $v\in B^n$, there is a unique $w\in B^d$ whose differential image cancels that of $v$, so $(v,w)$ is in the image of $M$; a vector of $M$ with first component zero has second component zero as well. Injectivity of $\mathrm d$ proves uniqueness in $M$.

Let $\eta_1,\ldots,\eta_n$ be the resulting basis of $M$ whose projected differentials are the standard basis of $B^n$. Write each $\eta_i$ as a fraction of a class represented by $f_i\in J$, with denominator $a^{k_i}$. Thus the classes of $f_i$ are $a^{k_i}\eta_i$, still a basis over $B$. Their square Jacobian on $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ is diagonal after passage to $B$, with entries $a^{k_i}$. In particular the image of $$\delta=\det(\partial f_i/\partial X_j)_{i,j=1}^n\in A$$ is a unit in $B$. Extend $f_1,\ldots,f_n$ to a finite generating list $f_1,\ldots,f_m$ of $J$. The finite module $$Q=(J/J^2)/\langle f_1,\ldots,f_n\rangle$$ has zero localization at $a$. A common power $a^L$ kills its finite generating list. For a polynomial lift $h\in P$ of $a$, this means $$h^L f_j\in(f_1,\ldots,f_n)+J^2\qquad(j>n).$$ All higher powers satisfy the same relation condition.

Since $\delta$ is a unit in $B$, choose $u\in A$ and $r\ge0$ with $\delta(u/a^r)=1$ in $B$. The equality in this localization supplies $v\ge0$ such that $$a^v(\delta u-a^r)=0\quad\hbox{in }A, \qquad a^{r+v}=\delta(a^v u).$$ Increase the exponent to a positive $K$ by multiplying this equality by an additional power of $a$ if necessary. This gives $a^K=\delta u_0$ in $A$, without cancelling a power of a possible zero divisor. Every $e\ge\max(K,L,1)$ then satisfies both D.3e1 and D.3e2 for the presentation $A=P/J$, with $c=n$ and the selected variables $X_i$. This proves the forward direction, including $n=0$, when $\delta$ is the empty determinant $1$.

Conversely, suppose $a^r$ is elementary for some $r\ge1$. Inverting $a^r$ is the same as inverting $a$, since $a^{-1}=a^{r-1}(a^r)^{-1}$. Part (c), applied to $a^r$, proves that $B$ is standard smooth, hence smooth. Take its elementary presentation $A=R[x_1,\ldots,x_N]/I$ with $I=(g_1,\ldots,g_m)$ and selected minor on $x_1,\ldots,x_c$. In $B$, D.3e2 makes every remaining conormal class a combination of the first $c$. Therefore $$\Omega_{B/R}=B^N/\langle\mathrm dg_1,\ldots,\mathrm dg_c\rangle.$$ The selected $c\times c$ Jacobian block is invertible. Subtracting a unique combination of these $c$ differential rows eliminates the first $c$ coordinates of any vector in $B^N$; a combination with those coordinates zero has all its coefficients zero. Hence the images of $\mathrm dx_{c+1},\ldots,\mathrm dx_N$ form a basis of this quotient. Their representatives are elements of $A$. The forward direction now proves that every sufficiently large power is elementary. This proves (f). ∎

Why standard smoothness alone is insufficient. Take $$R=\mathbf Z,\qquad A=\mathbf Z[t^2,t^3]\subset\mathbf Z[t],\qquad a=t^2.$$ This algebra has the finite presentation $$A\cong\mathbf Z[X,Y]/(Y^2-X^3),\qquad X\longmapsto t^2,\quad Y\longmapsto t^3.$$ Indeed division by the monic polynomial $Y^2-X^3$ writes every class uniquely as $p(X)+Yq(X)$. After substitution, the first summand has even exponents and the second has odd exponents at least $3$; their disjoint monomials prove injectivity. The image is precisely the indicated subalgebra.

Inverting $a$ gives $$B=A_a=\mathbf Z[t,t^{-1}],\qquad t=Y/X,\quad t^{-1}=Y/X^2.$$ These identities follow from $Y^2=X^3$ and give both inclusions with the Laurent ring. The presentation $B=\mathbf Z[T,U]/(TU-1)$ is standard smooth: select $U$ for its one equation, whose derivative is the unit $T$. Every derivation of $B$ is uniquely determined by its value on $t$, with $\mathrm d(t^{-1})=-t^{-2}\mathrm dt$. Thus $\Omega_{B/\mathbf Z}=B\,\mathrm dt$.

The units of $\mathbf Z[t,t^{-1}]$ are exactly $\pm t^k$. To check this, the lowest and highest nonzero exponents of a product add, since their coefficients are nonzero products in the domain $\mathbf Z$. For a product equal to $1$, each factor must therefore have width zero and be a monomial; its integer coefficient must be $1$ or $-1$.

Every $b\in A$ has the form $b_0+\sum_{k\ge2}b_k t^k$, with integer coefficients and a finite sum. Consequently $$\mathrm db=\left(\sum_{k\ge2}k b_k t^{k-1}\right)\mathrm dt.$$ This coefficient cannot be a unit: if it were $\pm t^j$, necessarily $j\ge1$, and its sole coefficient would require $(j+1)b_{j+1}=\pm1$, impossible in $\mathbf Z$. A basis of the free rank-one module $B\,\mathrm dt$ must contain one generator; tensoring with $\mathbf Q(t)$ verifies that its length is one. Hence it has no basis consisting of differentials of elements of $A$. By the converse in (f), no positive power of $a$ is elementary standard, despite standard smoothness of $B$.

There is no conflict with (e). In the original cusp presentation the two one-by-one minors are $-3X^2$ and $2Y$, and in $A$ $$X^3=(-X)(-3X^2)+(-Y)(2Y).$$ The relation condition is empty because there is only one equation. Thus $a^3$, and every $a^e$ with $e\ge3$ after multiplication by $a^{e-3}$, is strictly standard. This exact example distinguishes the sum-of-minors condition from the single-minor condition over the same arbitrary base.

The lifting problem

The goal in this section is to prove (Proposition D.18) that the collection of algebras which are filtered colimits of smooth algebras is closed under infinitesimal flat deformations. The proof is elementary and only uses the results on presentations of smooth algebras from Section § presentations.

Lemma D.16: lift once

Adapted from the Stacks project, smoothing.tex, lines 1237–1305.

Let $R \to \Lambda$ be a ring map. Let $I \subset R$ be an ideal. Assume that

  1. $I^2 = 0$, and

  2. $\Lambda/I\Lambda$ is a filtered colimit of smooth $R/I$-algebras.

Let $\varphi : A \to \Lambda$ be an $R$-algebra map with $A$ of finite presentation over $R$. Then there exists a factorization

$$ A \to B/J \to \Lambda $$

where $B$ is a smooth $R$-algebra and $J \subset IB$ is a finitely generated ideal.

Proof. Choose a factorization

$$ A/IA \to \bar B \to \Lambda/I\Lambda $$

with $\bar B$ standard smooth over $R/I$; this is possible by assumption and Lemma D.13. Write

$$ \bar B = A/IA[t_1, \ldots, t_r]/(\bar g_1, \ldots, \bar g_s) $$

and say $\bar B \to \Lambda/I\Lambda$ maps $t_i$ to the class of $\lambda_i$ modulo $I\Lambda$. Choose $g_1, \ldots, g_s \in A[t_1, \ldots, t_r]$ lifting $\bar g_1, \ldots, \bar g_s$. Write $\varphi(g_i)(\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_r) = \sum \epsilon_{ij} \mu_{ij}$ for some $\epsilon_{ij} \in I$ and $\mu_{ij} \in \Lambda$. Define

$$ A' = A[t_1, \ldots, t_r, \delta_{i, j}]/ (g_i - \sum \epsilon_{ij} \delta_{ij}) $$

and consider the map

$$ A' \longrightarrow \Lambda,\quad a \longmapsto \varphi(a),\quad t_i \longmapsto \lambda_i,\quad \delta_{ij} \longmapsto \mu_{ij} $$

We have

$$ A'/IA' = A/IA[t_1, \ldots, t_r]/(\bar g_1, \ldots, \bar g_s)[\delta_{ij}] \cong \bar B[\delta_{ij}] $$

This is a standard smooth algebra over $R/I$ as $\bar B$ is standard smooth. Choose a presentation $A'/IA' = R/I[x_1, \ldots, x_n]/(\bar f_1, \ldots, \bar f_c)$ with $\det(\partial \bar f_j/\partial x_i)_{i, j = 1, \ldots, c}$ invertible in $A'/IA'$. Choose lifts $f_1, \ldots, f_c \in R[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$ of $\bar f_1, \ldots, \bar f_c$. Then

$$ B = R[x_1, \ldots, x_n, x_{n + 1}]/ (f_1, \ldots, f_c, x_{n + 1}\det(\partial f_j/\partial x_i)_{i, j = 1, \ldots, c} - 1) $$

is smooth over $R$. Since smooth ring maps are formally smooth (Algebra, Proposition AG-CA-17, Theorem 3.1 and the split conormal definition of smoothness in this draft) there exists an $R$-algebra map $B \to A'$ which is an isomorphism modulo $I$. Then $B \to A'$ is surjective by Nakayama's lemma (Algebra, Lemma F.10). Thus $A' = B/J$ with $J \subset IB$ finitely generated (see Algebra, Lemma F.44). ∎

Lemma D.17: lift twice

Adapted from the Stacks project, smoothing.tex, lines 1307–1371.

Let $R \to \Lambda$ be a ring map. Let $I \subset R$ be an ideal. Assume that

  1. $I^2 = 0$,

  2. $\Lambda/I\Lambda$ is a filtered colimit of smooth $R/I$-algebras, and

  3. $R \to \Lambda$ is flat.

Let $\varphi : B \to \Lambda$ be an $R$-algebra map with $B$ smooth over $R$. Let $J \subset IB$ be a finitely generated ideal such that $\varphi(J) = 0$. Then there exists $R$-algebra maps

$$ B \xrightarrow{\alpha} B' \xrightarrow{\beta} \Lambda $$

such that $B'$ is smooth over $R$, such that $\alpha(J) = 0$ and such that $\beta \circ \alpha = \varphi$.

Proof. If we can prove the lemma in case $J = (h)$, then we can prove the lemma by induction on the number of generators of $J$. Namely, suppose that $J$ can be generated by $n$ elements $h_1, \ldots, h_n$ and the lemma holds for all cases where $J$ is generated by $n - 1$ elements. Then we apply the case $n = 1$ to produce $B \to B' \to \Lambda$ where the first map kills $h_n$. Then we let $J'$ be the ideal of $B'$ generated by the images of $h_1, \ldots, h_{n - 1}$ and we apply the case for $n - 1$ to produce $B' \to B'' \to \Lambda$. It is easy to verify that $B \to B'' \to \Lambda$ does the job.

Assume $J = (h)$ and write $h = \sum \epsilon_i b_i$ for some $\epsilon_i \in I$ and $b_i \in B$. Note that $0 = \varphi(h) = \sum \epsilon_i \varphi(b_i)$. As $\Lambda$ is flat over $R$, the equational criterion for flatness (Algebra, Lemma AG-CA-07, Theorem 5.1) implies that we can find $\lambda_j \in \Lambda$, $j = 1, \ldots, m$ and $a_{ij} \in R$ such that $\varphi(b_i) = \sum_j a_{ij} \lambda_j$ and $\sum_i \epsilon_i a_{ij} = 0$. Set

$$ C = B[x_1, \ldots, x_m]/(b_i - \sum a_{ij} x_j) $$

with $C \to \Lambda$ given by $\varphi$ and $x_j \mapsto \lambda_j$. Choose a factorization

$$ C \to B'/J' \to \Lambda $$

as in Lemma D.16. Since $B$ is smooth over $R$ we can lift the map $B \to C \to B'/J'$ to a map $\alpha : B \to B'$. Then $\varphi = \beta \circ \alpha$. To finish the proof we check that $\alpha(h) = 0$. Namely, the fact that $\alpha$ lifts $B \to C \to B'/J'$ implies that

$$ \alpha(b_i) = \sum a_{ij} \xi_j + \theta_i $$

for some $\xi_j \in B'$ and $\theta_i \in J' \subset IB'$. Hence we see that

$$ \alpha(h) = \alpha(\sum \epsilon_i b_i) = \sum \epsilon_i a_{ij} \xi_j + \sum \epsilon_i \theta_i = 0 $$

because of the relations above and the fact that $I^2 = 0$. ∎

Proposition D.18: lift

Adapted from the Stacks project, smoothing.tex, lines 1373–1407.

Let $R \to \Lambda$ be a ring map. Let $I \subset R$ be an ideal. Assume that

  1. $I$ is nilpotent,

  2. $\Lambda/I\Lambda$ is a filtered colimit of smooth $R/I$-algebras, and

  3. $R \to \Lambda$ is flat.

Then $\Lambda$ is a filtered colimit of smooth $R$-algebras.

Proof. First prove the assertion when $I^2=0$. For a finitely presented $R$-algebra $A$ and an $R$-algebra map $A\to\Lambda$, D.16 gives a factorization $A\to B/J\to\Lambda$, where $B$ is smooth over $R$ and $J\subset IB$ is finitely generated. The induced map $B\to\Lambda$ kills $J$. All hypotheses of D.17 hold: the same ideal has square zero, the quotient target is the assumed smooth colimit, and $\Lambda$ is flat over $R$. That lemma gives $B\to B'\to\Lambda$ with $B'$ smooth and $J$ killed in $B'$. Consequently $A\to B/J\to B'\to\Lambda$ is the required smooth factorization. Criterion F.90 proves the square-zero assertion.

Now induct on an integer $n\geq1$ such that $I^n=0$. If $n=1$, then $I=0$ and the conclusion is the hypothesis. For $n\geq2$, put $J=I^{n-1}$. We have $J^2=0$, since $2n-2\geq n$. Set $\bar R=R/J$, $\bar\Lambda=\Lambda/J\Lambda$ and $\bar I=I/J$. Then $\bar I^{n-1}=0$ and $$\bar\Lambda/\bar I\bar\Lambda\cong\Lambda/I\Lambda.$$ The map $\bar R\to\bar\Lambda$ is flat by base change: for a $\bar R$-module $M$, $M\otimes_{\bar R}\bar\Lambda\cong M\otimes_R\Lambda$, so its tensor functor preserves exact sequences. The induction hypothesis therefore makes $\bar\Lambda$ a filtered colimit of smooth $\bar R$-algebras. Apply the already proved square-zero case to $J\subset R$ and the original flat map $R\to\Lambda$. It gives the required smooth colimit over $R$, completing the induction. ∎

The lifting lemma

The next lemma constructs a finite presentation lifting the smooth locus.

Lemma D.19: lifting

Adapted from the Stacks project, smoothing.tex, lines 1420–1651.

Let $R$ be a Noetherian ring. Let $\Lambda$ be an $R$-algebra. Let $\pi \in R$ and assume that $\text{Ann}_R(\pi) = \text{Ann}_R(\pi^2)$ and $\text{Ann}_\Lambda(\pi) = \text{Ann}_\Lambda(\pi^2)$. Suppose we have $R$-algebra maps $R/\pi^2R \to \bar C \to \Lambda/\pi^2\Lambda$ with $\bar C$ of finite presentation. Then there exists an $R$-algebra homomorphism $D \to \Lambda$ and a commutative diagram

$$ \begin{gathered} R/\pi^2R \xrightarrow{} \bar C \\ R/\pi^2R \xrightarrow{} R/\pi R \\ \bar C \xrightarrow{} \Lambda/\pi^2\Lambda \\ \bar C \xrightarrow{} D/\pi D \\ \Lambda/\pi^2\Lambda \xrightarrow{} \Lambda/\pi \Lambda \\ R/\pi R \xrightarrow{} D/\pi D \\ D/\pi D \xrightarrow{} \Lambda/\pi \Lambda \end{gathered} $$

with the following properties

  1. (a) $D$ is of finite presentation,

  2. (b) $R \to D$ is smooth at any prime $\mathfrak q$ with $\pi \not \in \mathfrak q$,

  3. (c) $R \to D$ is smooth at any prime $\mathfrak q$ with $\pi \in \mathfrak q$ lying over a prime of $\bar C$ where $R/\pi^2 R \to \bar C$ is smooth, and

  4. (d) $\bar C/\pi \bar C \to D/\pi D$ is smooth at any prime lying over a prime of $\bar C$ where $R/\pi^2R \to \bar C$ is smooth.

Proof. We choose a presentation

$$ \bar C = R[x_1, \ldots, x_n]/(f_1, \ldots, f_m) $$

We also denote $I = (f_1, \ldots, f_m)$ and $\bar I$ the image of $I$ in $R/\pi^2R[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$. The finite presentation makes $\bar C$ Noetherian by AG-CA-03, Theorem 2.1, and its spectrum is Noetherian by Proposition 2.2 of that lesson. The smooth locus is open. Its principal smooth charts have a finite subcover: among their finite unions choose a maximal one using the ascending-chain condition on open sets; adjoining any other chart cannot enlarge it, so that union already covers the entire locus. This also includes the empty smooth locus. Applying Lemma D.2 we may choose a finite list of elements $a_1, \ldots, a_r \in R[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$ such that

  1. the union of the open subspaces $\operatorname{Spec}(\bar C_{a_k}) \subset \operatorname{Spec}(\bar C)$ cover the smooth locus of $R/\pi^2 R \to \bar C$, and

  2. for each $k = 1, \ldots, r$ there exists a finite subset $E_k \subset \{1, \ldots, m\}$ such that $(\bar I/\bar I^2)_{a_k}$ is freely generated by the classes of $f_j$, $j \in E_k$.

Set $I_k = (f_j, j \in E_k) \subset I$ and denote $\bar I_k$ the image of $I_k$ in $R/\pi^2R[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$. By (2) and Nakayama's lemma we see that $(\bar I/\bar I_k)_{a_k}$ is annihilated by $1 + b'_k$ for some $b'_k \in \bar I_{a_k}$. Suppose $b'_k$ is the image of $b_k/(a_k)^N$ for some $b_k \in I$ and some integer $N$. After replacing $a_k$ by $a_k((a_k)^N + b_k)$ we get

  1. (3) $(\bar I_k)_{a_k} = (\bar I)_{a_k}$.

Thus, after possibly replacing $a_k$ by a high power, we may write

  1. (4) $a_k f_\ell = \sum\nolimits_{j \in E_k} h_{k, \ell}^jf_j + \pi^2 g_{k, \ell}$

for any $\ell \in \{1, \ldots, m\}$ and some $h_{k, \ell}^j, g_{k, \ell} \in R[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$. If $\ell \in E_k$ we choose $h_{k, \ell}^j = a_k\delta_{\ell, j}$ (Kronecker delta) and $g_{k, \ell} = 0$. Set

$$ D = R[x_1, \ldots, x_n, z_1, \ldots, z_m]/ (f_j - \pi z_j, p_{k, \ell}). $$

Here $j \in \{1, \ldots, m\}$, $k \in \{1, \ldots, r\}$, $\ell \in \{1, \ldots, m\}$, and

$$ p_{k, \ell} = a_k z_\ell - \sum\nolimits_{j \in E_k} h_{k, \ell}^j z_j - \pi g_{k, \ell}. $$

Note that for $\ell \in E_k$ we have $p_{k, \ell} = 0$ by our choices above.

The map $R \to D$ is the given one. Say $\bar C \to \Lambda/\pi^2\Lambda$ maps $x_i$ to the class of $\lambda_i$ modulo $\pi^2$. For an element $f \in R[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$ we denote $f(\lambda) \in \Lambda$ the result of substituting $\lambda_i$ for $x_i$. Then we know that $f_j(\lambda) = \pi^2 \mu_j$ for some $\mu_j \in \Lambda$. Define $D \to \Lambda$ by the rules $x_i \mapsto \lambda_i$ and $z_j \mapsto \pi\mu_j$. This is well defined because

$$ \begin{aligned} p_{k, \ell} & \mapsto a_k(\lambda) \pi \mu_\ell - \sum\nolimits_{j \in E_k} h_{k, \ell}^j(\lambda) \pi \mu_j - \pi g_{k, \ell}(\lambda) \\ & = \pi\left(a_k(\lambda) \mu_\ell - \sum\nolimits_{j \in E_k} h_{k, \ell}^j(\lambda) \mu_j - g_{k, \ell}(\lambda)\right) \end{aligned} $$

Substituting $x_i = \lambda_i$ in (4) above we see that the expression inside the brackets is annihilated by $\pi^2$, hence it is annihilated by $\pi$ as we have assumed $\text{Ann}_\Lambda(\pi) = \text{Ann}_\Lambda(\pi^2)$. The map $\bar C \to D/\pi D$ is determined by $x_i \mapsto x_i$ (clearly well defined). Thus we are done if we can prove (b), (c), and (d).

Using (4) we obtain the following key equality

$$ \begin{aligned} \pi p_{k, \ell} & = \pi a_k z_\ell - \sum\nolimits_{j \in E_k} \pi h_{k, \ell}^jz_j - \pi^2 g_{k, \ell} \\ & = - a_k (f_\ell - \pi z_\ell) + a_k f_\ell + \sum\nolimits_{j \in E_k} h_{k, \ell}^j (f_j - \pi z_j) - \sum\nolimits_{j \in E_k} h_{k, \ell}^j f_j - \pi^2 g_{k, \ell} \\ & = -a_k(f_\ell - \pi z_\ell) + \sum\nolimits_{j \in E_k} h_{k, \ell}^j(f_j - \pi z_j) \end{aligned} $$

The end result is an element of the ideal generated by $f_j - \pi z_j$. In particular, we see that $D[1/\pi]$ is isomorphic to $R[1/\pi][x_1, \ldots, x_n, z_1, \ldots, z_m]/(f_j - \pi z_j)$ which is isomorphic to $R[1/\pi][x_1, \ldots, x_n]$ hence smooth over $R$. This proves (b).

For fixed $k \in \{1, \ldots, r\}$ consider the ring

$$ D_k = R[x_1, \ldots, x_n, z_1, \ldots, z_m]/ (f_j - \pi z_j, j \in E_k, p_{k, \ell}) $$

The number of equations is $m = |E_k| + (m - |E_k|)$ as $p_{k, \ell}$ is zero if $\ell \in E_k$. Also, note that

$$ \begin{aligned} (D_k/\pi D_k)_{a_k} & = R/\pi R[x_1, \ldots, x_n, 1/a_k, z_1, \ldots, z_m]/ (f_j, j \in E_k, p_{k, \ell}) \\ & = (\bar C/\pi \bar C)_{a_k}[z_1, \ldots, z_m]/ (a_kz_\ell - \sum\nolimits_{j \in E_k} h_{k, \ell}^j z_j) \\ & \cong (\bar C/\pi \bar C)_{a_k}[z_j, j \in E_k] \end{aligned} $$

In particular $(D_k/\pi D_k)_{a_k}$ is smooth over $(\bar C/\pi \bar C)_{a_k}$. By our choice of $a_k$ we have that $(\bar C/\pi \bar C)_{a_k}$ is smooth over $R/\pi R$ of relative dimension $n - |E_k|$, see (2). Hence for a prime $\mathfrak q_k \subset D_k$ containing $\pi$ and lying over $\operatorname{Spec}(\bar C_{a_k})$ the fibre ring of $R \to D_k$ is smooth at $\mathfrak q_k$ of dimension $n$. Thus $R \to D_k$ is syntomic at $\mathfrak q_k$ by our count of the number of equations above, see Algebra, Lemma F.66. Hence $R \to D_k$ is smooth at $\mathfrak q_k$, see Algebra, Lemma F.45.

To finish the proof, let $\mathfrak q \subset D$ be a prime containing $\pi$ lying over a prime where $R/\pi^2 R \to \bar C$ is smooth. Then $a_k \not \in \mathfrak q$ for some $k$ by (1). We will show that the surjection $D_k \to D$ induces an isomorphism on local rings at $\mathfrak q$. Since we know that the ring maps $\bar C/\pi \bar C \to D_k/\pi D_k$ and $R \to D_k$ are smooth at the corresponding prime $\mathfrak q_k$ by the preceding paragraph this will prove (c) and (d) and thus finish the proof.

First, note that for any $\ell$ the equation $\pi p_{k, \ell} = -a_k(f_\ell - \pi z_\ell) + \sum_{j \in E_k} h_{k, \ell}^j (f_j - \pi z_j)$ proved above shows that $f_\ell - \pi z_\ell$ maps to zero in $(D_k)_{a_k}$ and in particular in $(D_k)_{\mathfrak q_k}$. Reducing relations (4) modulo $\pi^2$ kills their $\pi^2g_{k,\ell}$ term. They therefore give $a_k\bar f_\ell=\sum_{j\in E_k}\bar h_{k,\ell}^j\bar f_j$ in $\bar I/\bar I^2$; this assertion is made in the reduced conormal module, not in $I/I^2$. Since $(\bar I_k/\bar I_k^2)_{a_k}$ is free on $f_j$, $j \in E_k$ we see that

$$ a_{k'} h_{k, \ell}^j - \sum\nolimits_{j' \in E_{k'}} h_{k', \ell}^{j'} h_{k, j'}^j $$

is zero in $\bar C_{a_k}$ for every $k, k', \ell$ and $j \in E_k$. Hence we can find a large integer $N$ such that

$$ a_k^N\left( a_{k'} h_{k, \ell}^j - \sum\nolimits_{j' \in E_{k'}} h_{k', \ell}^{j'} h_{k, j'}^j \right) $$

is in $I_k + \pi^2R[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$. Computing modulo $\pi$ we have

$$ \begin{aligned} & a_kp_{k', \ell} - a_{k'}p_{k, \ell} + \sum h_{k', \ell}^{j'} p_{k, j'} \\ & = - a_k \sum h_{k', \ell}^{j'} z_{j'} + a_{k'} \sum h_{k, \ell}^j z_j + \sum h_{k', \ell}^{j'} a_k z_{j'} - \sum \sum h_{k', \ell}^{j'} h_{k, j'}^j z_j \\ & = \sum \left( a_{k'} h_{k, \ell}^j - \sum h_{k', \ell}^{j'} h_{k, j'}^j \right) z_j \end{aligned} $$

with Einstein summation convention. Combining with the above we see $a_k^{N + 1} p_{k', \ell}$ is contained in the ideal generated by $I_k$ and $\pi$ in $R[x_1, \ldots, x_n, z_1, \ldots, z_m]$. Thus $p_{k', \ell}$ maps into $\pi (D_k)_{a_k}$. On the other hand, the equation

$$ \pi p_{k', \ell} = -a_{k'} (f_\ell - \pi z_\ell) + \sum\nolimits_{j' \in E_{k'}} h_{k', \ell}^{j'}(f_{j'} - \pi z_{j'}) $$

shows that $\pi p_{k', \ell}$ is zero in $(D_k)_{a_k}$. Put $T=(D_k)_{\mathfrak q_k}$, already proved smooth and hence flat over $R$. For $r=1,2$, tensor the exact kernel sequence $$0\longrightarrow\operatorname{Ann}_R(\pi^r)\longrightarrow R\xrightarrow{\pi^r}R$$ with $T$. Exactness identifies its left image with $\operatorname{Ann}_T(\pi^r)$. The equality of the two original annihilator submodules therefore gives $\operatorname{Ann}_T(\pi)=\operatorname{Ann}_T(\pi^2)$.

We have proved that the image $p$ of each $p_{k',\ell}$ lies in $\pi T$ and satisfies $\pi p=0$. Write $p=\pi u$. Then $\pi^2u=0$, so the annihilator equality gives $\pi u=0$, which is $p=0$. The relations $f_\ell-\pi z_\ell$ already vanish in $T$, as proved above. These and the $p_{k',\ell}$ are exactly all additional relations of the surjection $D_k\to D$. Its localized kernel is consequently zero, giving $D_{\mathfrak q}\cong T$. The previously proved smoothness of $R\to T$ and of the corresponding quotient chart proves (c) and (d). ∎

The desingularization lemma

The next construction improves the singular ideal.

Lemma D.20: desingularize

Adapted from the Stacks project, smoothing.tex, lines 1664–1809.

Let $R$ be a Noetherian ring. Let $\Lambda$ be an $R$-algebra. Let $\pi \in R$ and assume that $\text{Ann}_\Lambda(\pi) = \text{Ann}_\Lambda(\pi^2)$. Let $A \to \Lambda$ be an $R$-algebra map with $A$ of finite presentation. Assume

  1. the image of $\pi$ is strictly standard in $A$ over $R$, and

  2. there exists a section $\rho : A/\pi^4 A \to R/\pi^4 R$ which is compatible with the map to $\Lambda/\pi^4 \Lambda$.

Then we can find $R$-algebra maps $A \to B \to \Lambda$ with $B$ of finite presentation such that $\mathfrak a B \subset H_{B/R}$ where $\mathfrak a = \text{Ann}_R(\text{Ann}_R(\pi^2)/\text{Ann}_R(\pi))$.

Proof. Choose a presentation

$$ A = R[x_1, \ldots, x_n]/(f_1, \ldots, f_m) $$

and $0 \leq c \leq \min(n, m)$ such that (D.3s1: strict Jacobian-minor condition) holds for $\pi$ and such that

$$ \pi f_{c + j} \in (f_1, \ldots, f_c) + (f_1, \ldots, f_m)^2 $$

for $j = 1, \ldots, m - c$. Say $\rho$ maps $x_i$ to the class of $r_i \in R$. Then we can replace $x_i$ by $x_i - r_i$. Hence we may assume $\rho(x_i) = 0$ in $R/\pi^4 R$. This implies that $f_j(0) \in \pi^4R$ and that $A \to \Lambda$ maps $x_i$ to $\pi^4\lambda_i$ for some $\lambda_i \in \Lambda$. Write

$$ f_j = f_j(0) + \sum\nolimits_{i = 1, \ldots, n} r_{ji} x_i + \text{h.o.t.} $$

This implies that the constant term of $\partial f_j/\partial x_i$ is $r_{ji}$. Apply $\rho$ to (D.3s1: strict Jacobian-minor condition) for $\pi$ and we see that

$$ \pi = \sum\nolimits_{I \subset \{1, \ldots, n\},\ |I| = c} r_I \det(r_{ji})_{j = 1, \ldots, c,\ i \in I} \bmod \pi^4R $$

for some $r_I \in R$. Thus we have

$$ u\pi = \sum\nolimits_{I \subset \{1, \ldots, n\},\ |I| = c} r_I \det(r_{ji})_{j = 1, \ldots, c,\ i \in I} $$

for some $u \in 1 + \pi^3R$. By Algebra, Lemma F.70 this implies there exists a $n \times c$ matrix $(s_{ik})$ such that

$$ u\pi \delta_{jk} = \sum\nolimits_{i = 1, \ldots, n} r_{ji}s_{ik}\quad \text{for all } j, k = 1, \ldots, c $$

(Kronecker delta). We introduce auxiliary variables $v_1, \ldots, v_c, w_1, \ldots, w_n$ and we set

$$ h_i = x_i - \pi^2 \sum\nolimits_{j = 1, \ldots c} s_{ij} v_j - \pi^3 w_i $$

In the following we will use that

$$ R[x_1, \ldots, x_n, v_1, \ldots, v_c, w_1, \ldots, w_n]/ (h_1, \ldots, h_n) = R[v_1, \ldots, v_c, w_1, \ldots, w_n] $$

without further mention. In $R[x_1, \ldots, x_n, v_1, \ldots, v_c, w_1, \ldots, w_n]/ (h_1, \ldots, h_n)$ we have

$$ \begin{aligned} f_j & = f_j(x_1 - h_1, \ldots, x_n - h_n) \\ & = \pi^2 \sum\nolimits_{k = 1}^c \left(\sum\nolimits_{i = 1}^n r_{ji} s_{ik}\right) v_k + \pi^3 \sum\nolimits_{i = 1}^n r_{ji}w_i \bmod \pi^4 \\ & = \pi^3 v_j + \pi^3 \sum\nolimits_{i = 1}^n r_{ji}w_i \bmod \pi^4 \end{aligned} $$

for $1 \leq j \leq c$. Hence we can choose elements $g_j \in R[v_1, \ldots, v_c, w_1, \ldots, w_n]$ such that $g_j = v_j + \sum r_{ji}w_i \bmod \pi$ and such that $f_j = \pi^3 g_j$ in $Q/(h_1,\ldots,h_n)$, where

$$ Q=R[x_1,\ldots,x_n,v_1,\ldots,v_c,w_1,\ldots,w_n]. $$

We set

$$ B = R[x_1, \ldots, x_n, v_1, \ldots, v_c, w_1, \ldots, w_n]/ (f_1, \ldots, f_m, h_1, \ldots, h_n, g_1, \ldots, g_c). $$

The map $A \to B$ is clear. We define $B \to \Lambda$ by mapping $x_i \to \pi^4\lambda_i$, $v_i \mapsto 0$, and $w_i \mapsto \pi \lambda_i$. Then it is clear that the elements $f_j$ and $h_i$ are mapped to zero in $\Lambda$. Moreover, it is clear that $g_i$ is mapped to an element $t$ of $\pi\Lambda$ such that $\pi^3t = 0$ (as $f_i = \pi^3 g_i$ modulo the ideal generated by the $h$'s). The assumed annihilator equality implies equality with every positive power: if $\pi^ru=0$ with $r\geq2$, apply the equality to $\pi^{r-2}u$ to get $\pi^{r-1}u=0$, and repeat. Here $t=\pi u$ and $\pi^3t=0$, so $\pi^4u=0$ and the same induction gives $\pi u=0$. Thus $t=0$. Thus we are done if we can prove the statement about smoothness.

Note that $B_\pi \cong A_\pi[v_1, \ldots, v_c]$ because the equations $g_i = 0$ are implied by $f_i = 0$. Hence $B_\pi$ is smooth over $R$ as $A_\pi$ is smooth over $R$ by the assumption that $\pi$ is strictly standard in $A$ over $R$, see Lemma D.5.

Set $B' = R[v_1, \ldots, v_c, w_1, \ldots, w_n]/(g_1, \ldots, g_c)$. As $g_i = v_i + \sum r_{ji}w_i \bmod \pi$ we see that $B'/\pi B' = R/\pi R[w_1, \ldots, w_n]$. Hence $R \to B'$ is smooth of relative dimension $n$ at every point of $V(\pi)$ by Algebra, Lemmas F.66 and F.45 (the first lemma shows it is syntomic at those primes, in particular flat, whereupon the second lemma shows it is smooth).

Let $\mathfrak q\subset B$ contain $\pi$ and avoid an element $r\in\mathfrak a$. Put $\mathfrak q'=B'\cap\mathfrak q$ and $T=(B')_{\mathfrak q'}$. The preceding paragraph proves that $T$ is smooth and therefore flat over $R$. The surjection $T\to B_{\mathfrak q}$ has kernel generated by the images $F_j$ of $f_{c+j}$: the $h_i$ have already eliminated the $x_i$, and the first $c$ equations $f_i=\pi^3g_i$ are already zero in $B'$.

Every $F_j$ lies in $\pi^2T$, because the substituted $x_i$ are divisible by $\pi^2$ and the constant terms of the $f_i$ lie in $\pi^4R$. The strict relation condition D.3s2, after the first $c$ equations vanish, gives $$\pi F_j=\sum_{a,b} b_{j,a,b}F_aF_b.$$ For the finite ideal $M=(\pi F_j)_j\subset T$, this implies $M\subset\pi M$, since each first factor $F_a$ is divisible by $\pi^2$. The reverse inclusion is automatic, so $M=\pi M$. The element $\pi$ is in the maximal ideal of the Noetherian local ring $T$. Nakayama's proved finite-module form F.10 gives $M=0$. Thus $\pi F_j=0$ for every $j$.

Flatness identifies the two multiplication kernels and their quotient: $$\bigl(\operatorname{Ann}_R(\pi^2)/\operatorname{Ann}_R(\pi)\bigr)\otimes_RT\cong\operatorname{Ann}_T(\pi^2)/\operatorname{Ann}_T(\pi).$$ Indeed, tensor the exact sequences $0\to\operatorname{Ann}_R(\pi^a)\to R\xrightarrow{\pi^a}R$ for $a=1,2$ and then their submodule quotient sequence. The element $r$ kills the original quotient and is invertible in $T$, so this quotient is zero. Write $F_j=\pi u_j$. Since $\pi F_j=0$, we have $\pi^2u_j=0$, and the annihilator equality gives $\pi u_j=0$, or $F_j=0$. The entire localized kernel vanishes; hence $B_{\mathfrak q}\cong T$ is smooth over $R$.

Primes avoiding $\pi$ are already smooth by the displayed description of $B_\pi$. At every remaining prime avoiding $\mathfrak aB$, the preceding argument applies to some $r\in\mathfrak a$ outside that prime. Thus every nonsmooth prime contains $\mathfrak aB$. Definition D.1 and the radical-prime criterion give $\mathfrak aB\subset H_{B/R}$. Explicitly, an element outside a radical ideal has all its powers outside that ideal. An ideal maximal among those containing the ideal and disjoint from those powers is prime: if two elements outside it had product inside it, the product of the two enlarged ideals would contain a power and still lie in it, a contradiction. Consequently that element is avoided by a prime containing the radical ideal. Applying this criterion proves the asserted inclusion. ∎

Lemma D.21: desingularize strictly standard

Adapted from the Stacks project, smoothing.tex, lines 1811–1859.

Let $R$ be a Noetherian ring. Let $\Lambda$ be an $R$-algebra. Let $\pi \in R$ and assume that $\text{Ann}_R(\pi) = \text{Ann}_R(\pi^2)$ and $\text{Ann}_\Lambda(\pi) = \text{Ann}_\Lambda(\pi^2)$. Let $A \to \Lambda$ and $D \to \Lambda$ be $R$-algebra maps with $A$ and $D$ of finite presentation. Assume

  1. $\pi$ is strictly standard in $A$ over $R$, and

  2. there exists an $R$-algebra map $A/\pi^4 A \to D/\pi^4 D$ compatible with the maps to $\Lambda/\pi^4 \Lambda$.

Then we can find an $R$-algebra map $B \to \Lambda$ with $B$ of finite presentation and $R$-algebra maps $A \to B$ and $D \to B$ compatible with the maps to $\Lambda$ such that $H_{D/R}B \subset H_{B/D}$ and $H_{D/R}B \subset H_{B/R}$.

Proof. The ring $D$ is Noetherian: it is a finitely presented algebra over the Noetherian ring $R$, by the Hilbert-basis and quotient proof in AG-CA-03, Theorem 2.1. Put $C=A\otimes_RD$. It is finitely presented over $D$, and multiplication of the two given images defines $C\to\Lambda$. Base change D.7 makes $\pi$ strictly standard in $C$ over $D$.

The given map $\phi\colon A/\pi^4A\to D/\pi^4D$ defines a section $$\rho\colon C/\pi^4C\cong(A/\pi^4A)\otimes_{R/\pi^4R}(D/\pi^4D)\longrightarrow D/\pi^4D,\qquad a\otimes d\longmapsto\phi(a)d.$$ It is the identity on the $D/\pi^4D$ factor. Compatibility with $\Lambda/\pi^4\Lambda$ follows from the compatibility assumed for $\phi$. Apply D.20 over the base $D$. This lemma requires the annihilator equality in $\Lambda$, which is a hypothesis here; it does not require such an equality in $D$. We obtain $C\to B\to\Lambda$, with $B$ finitely presented over $D$, and $$\mathfrak aB\subset H_{B/D},\qquad M=\operatorname{Ann}_D(\pi^2)/\operatorname{Ann}_D(\pi),\qquad\mathfrak a=\operatorname{Ann}_D(M).$$ Finite presentation over $R$ follows by substituting presentations: if $D=R[u]/(g)$ and $B=D[v]/(h)$ with all lists finite, lift the $h$ to polynomials $\widetilde h$ in $R[u,v]$ to get $B=R[u,v]/(g,\widetilde h)$. The two tensor-factor maps give the required compatible maps $A\to B$ and $D\to B$.

Let $\mathfrak q\subset D$ be a prime where $R\to D$ is smooth. Then $D_{\mathfrak q}$ is flat over $R$. Tensoring the two exact multiplication-kernel sequences, as in the final paragraph of D.19, gives equal annihilators of $\pi$ and $\pi^2$ in $D_{\mathfrak q}$. Localization is exact, so $M_{\mathfrak q}=0$.

Here is the needed global annihilator calculation. Both annihilator ideals in the Noetherian ring $D$ are finite modules, hence $M$ has finite generators $m_1,\ldots,m_v$. Since $m_i/1=0$ in $M_{\mathfrak q}$, there is $s_i\in D\setminus\mathfrak q$ with $s_im_i=0$. The product $s=\prod_i s_i$ kills every generator, so $s\in\mathfrak a\setminus\mathfrak q$. If $M=0$, take $s=1$. Thus for every prime $\mathfrak r\subset B$ above $\mathfrak q$, the inclusion $\mathfrak aB\subset H_{B/D}$ gives an element of $H_{B/D}$ outside $\mathfrak r$. By definition D.1, $D\to B$ is smooth there.

We have proved $D(H_{D/R}B)\subset D(H_{B/D})$. Therefore $H_{D/R}B\subset H_{B/D}$, since the latter ideal is radical. Indeed, if an element lies outside a radical ideal, a prime containing that ideal and avoiding the element is obtained by taking an ideal maximal among those disjoint from its powers; the maximal ideal is prime because the product of two enlarged ideals would otherwise meet those powers. Apply this fact to the two complementary closed sets. At the same primes, both successive maps are smooth, so smooth composition F.29 gives smoothness of $R\to B$. The same radical-ideal argument gives $H_{D/R}B\subset H_{B/R}$. ∎

Lemma D.22: desingularize lifting apply

Adapted from the Stacks project, smoothing.tex, lines 1861–1894.

Let $R$ be a Noetherian ring. Let $\Lambda$ be an $R$-algebra. Let $\pi \in R$ and assume that $\text{Ann}_R(\pi) = \text{Ann}_R(\pi^2)$ and $\text{Ann}_\Lambda(\pi) = \text{Ann}_\Lambda(\pi^2)$. Let $A \to \Lambda$ be an $R$-algebra map with $A$ of finite presentation and assume $\pi$ is strictly standard in $A$ over $R$. Let

$$ A/\pi^8A \to \bar C \to \Lambda/\pi^8\Lambda $$

be a factorization with $\bar C$ of finite presentation. Then we can find a factorization $A \to B \to \Lambda$ with $B$ of finite presentation such that $R_\pi \to B_\pi$ is smooth and such that

$$ H_{\bar C/(R/\pi^8 R)} \cdot \Lambda/\pi^8\Lambda \subset \sqrt{H_{B/R} \Lambda} \bmod \pi^8\Lambda. $$

Proof. First record the power calculation. For multiplication by $u$ on a module, $\ker u=\ker u^2$ implies $\ker u^a=\ker u$ for all $a\ge1$: if $u^{a+1}v=0$, then $u^{a-1}v\in\ker u^2=\ker u$, so $u^av=0$, and induction finishes. Apply this with $u=\pi$ on $R$ and on $\Lambda$. In particular the annihilators of $\pi^4$ and $\pi^8$ agree in both rings.

Apply D.19 with parameter $\pi^4$ and input $\bar C$, a finitely presented $R/\pi^8R$-algebra mapping to $\Lambda/\pi^8\Lambda$. It gives a finitely presented $R$-algebra $D\to\Lambda$ and a compatible map $$\bar C/\pi^4\bar C\longrightarrow D/\pi^4D\longrightarrow\Lambda/\pi^4\Lambda.$$ Its property (b) makes $D$ smooth at primes avoiding $\pi$. Property (c) makes it smooth at a prime containing $\pi$ whenever that prime's contraction through the displayed quotient map is a smooth point of $\bar C$ over $R/\pi^8R$.

The composite $A/\pi^4A\to\bar C/\pi^4\bar C\to D/\pi^4D$ is compatible with the given map to $\Lambda/\pi^4\Lambda$. Thus every hypothesis of D.21 holds, with the original strictly-standard parameter $\pi$ in $A$. It supplies a finitely presented $R$-algebra $B$, compatible factorizations $A\to B\to\Lambda$ and $D\to B\to\Lambda$, and $$H_{D/R}B\subset H_{B/R}.$$ At a prime of $B$ avoiding $\pi$, its contraction to $D$ is smooth, so it avoids $H_{D/R}$. The inclusion shows it also avoids $H_{B/R}$. Therefore every point of $B[1/\pi]$ is smooth, and F.67 proves the required global smoothness over $R[1/\pi]$.

Put $J=H_{B/R}\Lambda$ and let $\mathfrak l$ be any prime of $\Lambda$ containing $J$. Its contractions $\mathfrak b\subset B$ and $\mathfrak d\subset D$ contain the respective singular ideals. The preceding smoothness forces $\pi\in\mathfrak l$. Consequently $\mathfrak d$ defines a prime of $D/\pi^4D$ and a contraction $\mathfrak c$ to $\bar C/\pi^4\bar C$. If the corresponding prime of $\bar C$ were smooth over $R/\pi^8R$, D.19(c) would make $D$ smooth at $\mathfrak d$, a contradiction. Thus $H_{\bar C/(R/\pi^8R)}$ lies in that contracted prime. Compatibility of all maps makes its image in $\Lambda/\pi^8\Lambda$ lie in $\mathfrak l/\pi^8\Lambda$.

Every prime containing $J$ contains $\pi$, and the prime-intersection proof in D.5 gives $\pi\in\sqrt J$. It also gives the asserted inclusion after intersecting the primes $\mathfrak l$: the ideal extended from $H_{\bar C/(R/\pi^8R)}$ is contained in the image of $\sqrt J$ modulo $\pi^8\Lambda$. If there are no such primes, $\sqrt J=\Lambda$ and this assertion holds as well. This proves both conclusions at the original arbitrary-target scope. ∎

Warmup: reduction to a base field

In this section we apply the lemmas in the previous sections to prove that it suffices to prove the main result when the base ring is a field, see Lemma D.26.

Situation D.23: global

Adapted from the Stacks project, smoothing.tex, lines 1915–1918.

Here $R \to \Lambda$ is a regular ring map of Noetherian rings.

Let $R \to \Lambda$ be as in Situation D.23. We say PT holds for $R \to \Lambda$ if $\Lambda$ is a filtered colimit of smooth $R$-algebras.

Lemma D.24: product

Adapted from the Stacks project, smoothing.tex, lines 1925–1934.

Let $R_i \to \Lambda_i$, $i = 1, 2$ be as in Situation D.23. If PT holds for $R_i \to \Lambda_i$, $i = 1, 2$, then PT holds for $R_1 \times R_2 \to \Lambda_1 \times \Lambda_2$.

Proof. Write $\Lambda_i=\operatorname*{colim}_{a\in I_i} B_{i,a}$ with $I_i$ filtered and every $B_{i,a}$ smooth over $R_i$. The category $I_1\times I_2$ is filtered: nonemptiness, a common successor for two objects, and an equalizer for two parallel arrows are constructed in the two coordinates. The $R_1\times R_2$-algebra $B_{1,a}\times B_{2,b}$ is smooth, because its spectrum is the disjoint union of the two corresponding smooth spectra. The natural map

$$ \operatorname*{colim}_{(a,b)\in I_1\times I_2}(B_{1,a}\times B_{2,b}) \longrightarrow \Lambda_1\times\Lambda_2 $$

is surjective by choosing representatives of the two components, and injective because any equality of pairs becomes an equality at successors in each coordinate. It is a ring isomorphism, proving the assertion. ∎

Lemma D.25: delocalize base

Adapted from the Stacks project, smoothing.tex, lines 1936–2000.

Let $R \to A \to \Lambda$ be ring maps with $A$ of finite presentation over $R$. Let $S \subset R$ be a multiplicative set. Let $S^{-1}A \to B' \to S^{-1}\Lambda$ be a factorization with $B'$ smooth over $S^{-1}R$. Then we can find a factorization $A \to B \to \Lambda$ such that some $s \in S$ maps to an elementary standard element (Definition D.3) in $B$ over $R$.

Proof. If $0\in S$, take $B=A$ and $s=0$. The element $0$ is elementary standard with $c=0$: the empty determinant is $1$, its coefficient is $0$, and all relation conditions are $0=0$. Hence assume $0\notin S$.

By D.12, a standard smooth algebra with a retraction can replace $B'$ while preserving the factorization. Write $A=R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/(g_1,\ldots,g_t)$, with $x_i\mapsto\lambda_i\in\Lambda$. The prescribed-generator construction D.14 gives $$B'=S^{-1}R[x_1,\ldots,x_{n+m}]/(f_1,\ldots,f_c),$$ where $c\geq n$, the first $n$ variable classes are the given generator images, and the determinant $\Delta=\det(\partial f_j/\partial x_i)_{i,j=1,\ldots,c}$ is invertible in $B'$. Repeated prescribed images cause no difficulty: the proof of D.14 adds one equation $x_i-h_i$ for each entry of a finite list, and its identity Jacobian block remains invertible even if entries coincide.

For each added variable choose a representation of its image in $S^{-1}\Lambda$ with denominator $d_i\in S$. Replacing that variable by $d_ix_i$ makes its image $\lambda_i/1$ for some $\lambda_i\in\Lambda$. This is an invertible change of variables over $S^{-1}R$. By the chain rule it multiplies each selected Jacobian column by a unit, so the selected determinant stays invertible. Choose $u_j\in S$ clearing the coefficients of each transformed equation and replace $f_j$ by $u_jf_j$. Their ideal over $S^{-1}R$ is unchanged, and the determinant is multiplied by $\prod_j u_j$, another unit. Thus all $f_j$ now lie in $P=R[x_1,\ldots,x_{n+m}]$.

The inverse of the determinant in $B'$ has a polynomial representative. Consequently there are $b_0,\ldots,b_c\in S^{-1}P$ such that $$1=b_0\Delta+\sum_{j=1}^c b_jf_j\quad\text{in }S^{-1}P.$$ Choose $d\in S$ and polynomial representatives $c_j\in P$ with $c_j/1=db_j$ in $S^{-1}P$. The difference $d-c_0\Delta-\sum_j c_jf_j$ maps to zero in $S^{-1}P$, so some $e\in S$ kills it in $P$. Setting $s_0=ed$ and $a_j=ec_j\in P$ gives the exact identity $$s_0=a_0\Delta+\sum_{j=1}^c a_jf_j\quad\text{in }P.$$ This extra multiplier $e$ covers possible $S$-torsion in $P$.

Each $g_i$ is zero in $S^{-1}(P/(f_1,\ldots,f_c))$. The definition of equality in a localization gives $s_i\in S$ with $s_ig_i\in(f_1,\ldots,f_c)$ in $P$. Similarly, $f_j(\lambda)$ is zero in $S^{-1}\Lambda$, so choose $s'_j\in S$ with $s'_jf_j(\lambda)=0$ in $\Lambda$. Put $$h_j=s'_jf_j,\qquad B=P/(h_1,\ldots,h_c,g_1,\ldots,g_t),\qquad s=s_0\Bigl(\prod_{i=1}^t s_i\Bigr)\Bigl(\prod_{j=1}^c s'_j\Bigr).$$ The finite equations give finite presentation, the $g_i$ give $A\to B$, and $x_i\mapsto\lambda_i$ defines $B\to\Lambda$.

We verify both parts of definition D.3. Multiplying $s_ig_i=\sum_j v_{ij}f_j$ by $s/s_i$ expresses $sg_i$ in $(h_1,\ldots,h_c)$, since the multiplier contains every $s'_j$. Put $t_0=\prod_j s'_j$. Multiplying the exact determinant identity by $t_0$ gives $$s_0t_0=a_0\det(\partial h_j/\partial x_i)_{i,j=1,\ldots,c}+\sum_{j=1}^c a_j\Bigl(\prod_{\ell\ne j}s'_\ell\Bigr)h_j.$$ In $B$ the relation terms vanish. After multiplication by $\prod_i s_i$, the image of $s$ is the selected determinant times the image of $a_0\prod_i s_i$. Together with $sg_i\in(h_1,\ldots,h_c)$, this is exactly the elementary standard condition. Empty products are $1$ and the same calculation includes $c=0$. ∎

Lemma D.26: reduce to field

Adapted from the Stacks project, smoothing.tex, lines 2002–2063.

If for every Situation D.23 where $R$ is a field PT holds, then PT holds in general.

Proof. Assume PT for every regular map from a field to a Noetherian ring, and fix the regular Noetherian map $R\to\Lambda$. Each quotient map $R/I\to\Lambda/I\Lambda$ is regular by F.123, since $R/I$ is finite type over $R$. If any quotient fails PT, choose an ideal $I$ maximal among those failures; the ascending-chain condition on ideals guarantees such a choice. Replace the map by that quotient. We then have a map failing PT for which every nonzero further ideal gives a quotient satisfying PT. The zero ring has PT, since its only unital algebra is itself, so the new $R$ is nonzero.

This $R$ is reduced. Indeed, its nilradical $J$ is a finite ideal because $R$ is Noetherian. Choose nilpotent generators $a_i$ with $a_i^{n_i}=0$. Every monomial of total degree $1+\sum_i(n_i-1)$ in these generators has an exponent at least $n_i$, so that power of $J$ is zero. If $J\ne0$, the quotient by $J$ has PT by maximality. The original map is flat, so the full nilpotent lifting proof D.18 would then give PT for $R\to\Lambda$, a contradiction. Thus $J=0$.

Let $\mathfrak p_1,\ldots,\mathfrak p_t$ be the finite minimal primes of $R$, as proved in AG-CA-03, Proposition 2.2. Their intersection is zero. To justify this last assertion directly, an element not nilpotent has powers disjoint from the zero ideal; an ideal maximal among those disjoint from its powers is prime, by the product-of-enlarged-ideals argument used in D.21. Thus the intersection of all prime ideals is precisely the nilradical. Every prime contains a minimal prime, so intersecting minimal primes gives the same intersection.

Here is an explicit decomposition of the total fraction ring. Choose $y_i\in\bigcap_{j\ne i}\mathfrak p_j\setminus\mathfrak p_i$: for each $j\ne i$ choose an element of $\mathfrak p_j\setminus\mathfrak p_i$ and take their product; if $t=1$, take $y_1=1$. An element outside every minimal prime is a nonzerodivisor, since a product equal to zero can be tested in each domain $R/\mathfrak p_i$ and their intersection is zero. Conversely, any $r\in\mathfrak p_i$ satisfies $ry_i=0$ with $y_i\ne0$, so it is a zerodivisor. Hence the set $S$ of nonzerodivisors is exactly $R\setminus\bigcup_i\mathfrak p_i$.

Put $d=\sum_i y_i\in S$, $Q=S^{-1}R$ and $e_i=y_i/d\in Q$. Testing in the domains $R/\mathfrak p_i$ shows $e_ie_j=0$ for $i\ne j$, $e_i^2=e_i$ and $\sum_i e_i=1$. The fraction ring embeds in the product of the fraction fields of these domains: a fraction zero in every factor has numerator in $\bigcap_i\mathfrak p_i=0$. Thus multiplication and summation give inverse maps $Q\cong\prod_i e_iQ$. Each nonzero $e_ir/s$ has $r\notin\mathfrak p_i$. The element $$u=e_ir+(1-e_i)=\frac{y_ir+\sum_{j\ne i}y_j}{d}$$ is invertible in $Q$, because its numerator avoids every minimal prime. In the component $e_iQ$, the inverse of $e_ir/s$ is $e_isu^{-1}$. Therefore every $K_i=e_iQ$ is a field, proving $Q\cong\prod_i K_i$ with its full ring maps. This is the total-fraction decomposition needed here; no embedded-prime assertion is left implicit.

The localized map $Q\to\Lambda_Q=S^{-1}\Lambda$ is regular. Its rings are Noetherian by quotient/localization permanence in AG-CA-03, Theorem 2.1. Flatness follows directly from the tensor identity $M\otimes_Q\Lambda_Q\cong M\otimes_R\Lambda$ for $Q$-modules. A prime of $Q$ contracts to a prime $\mathfrak p\subset R$ disjoint from $S$, with the same residue field; the fibre is therefore exactly $\Lambda\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p)$, geometrically regular by the original hypothesis. The finite idempotents split $\Lambda_Q$ as $\prod_i\Lambda_i$, and each $K_i\to\Lambda_i$ has these same regular fibres and is flat. By the assumed field case and the finite-product proof D.24, PT holds for $Q\to\Lambda_Q$.

Fix any finitely presented $R$-algebra $A$ and a map $A\to\Lambda$. Its localized presentation is finite, so F.90 gives a factorization $S^{-1}A\to B'\to S^{-1}\Lambda$ with $B'$ smooth over $Q$. Delocalization D.25 gives $A\to A_1\to\Lambda$ with an element $\pi\in S$ elementary standard in $A_1/R$. Definition D.3 makes it strictly standard too. Replace the algebra to be factored by $A_1$.

Since $R$ is nonzero and $\pi$ is a nonzerodivisor, $\pi^8\ne0$. The nonzero ideal $\pi^8R$ thus gives PT for $R/\pi^8R\to\Lambda/\pi^8\Lambda$, including the possible unit case. Applying F.90 to $A_1/\pi^8A_1$ gives a smooth factorization through an algebra $\bar C$ over $R/\pi^8R$. Multiplication by every $\pi^r$ is injective on $R$. Flatness of $\Lambda$ preserves the exact sequence $0\to R\xrightarrow{\pi^r}R$, so it is injective on $\Lambda$ as well. In particular both annihilator equalities required by D.19 hold for its parameter $\pi^4$. That lemma gives a finitely presented $R$-algebra $D\to\Lambda$ and $$A_1/\pi^4A_1\longrightarrow\bar C/\pi^4\bar C\longrightarrow D/\pi^4D\longrightarrow\Lambda/\pi^4\Lambda.$$ The map $R\to D$ is smooth at primes avoiding $\pi$, by D.19(b), and at primes containing $\pi$, by D.19(c) and smoothness of the entire $\bar C$ chart. Finite presentation and these local smooth charts make $D$ smooth over $R$.

Apply D.21 to $A_1$, $D$ and the parameter $\pi$. Its annihilator hypotheses have just been proved, and the displayed factorization supplies its compatible quotient map. It gives $A_1\to B\to\Lambda$ with $B$ finitely presented and $H_{D/R}B\subset H_{B/R}$. Since $D$ is smooth, definition D.1 gives $H_{D/R}=D$. Therefore $H_{B/R}=B$, and $B$ is smooth over $R$. Composing with $A\to A_1$ supplies the smooth factorization for every $A$. F.90 gives PT, contradicting the chosen failure. No failing quotient exists, and PT holds for the original map. ∎

Local tricks

Situation D.27: local

Adapted from the Stacks project, smoothing.tex, lines 2078–2084.

We are given a Noetherian ring $R$ and an $R$-algebra map $A \to \Lambda$ and a prime $\mathfrak q \subset \Lambda$. We assume $A$ is of finite presentation over $R$. In this situation we denote $\mathfrak h_A = \sqrt{H_{A/R} \Lambda}$.

Let $R \to A \to \Lambda \supset \mathfrak q$ be as in Situation D.27. We say $R \to A \to \Lambda \supset \mathfrak q$ can be resolved if there exists a factorization $A \to B \to \Lambda$ with $B$ of finite presentation and $\mathfrak h_A \subset \mathfrak h_B \not \subset \mathfrak q$. In this case we will call the factorization $A \to B \to \Lambda$ a resolution of $R \to A \to \Lambda \supset \mathfrak q$.

Lemma D.28: lift solution

Adapted from the Stacks project, smoothing.tex, lines 2096–2145.

Let $R \to A \to \Lambda \supset \mathfrak q$ be as in Situation D.27. Let $r \geq 1$ and $\pi_1, \ldots, \pi_r \in R$ map to elements of $\mathfrak q$. Assume

  1. for $i = 1, \ldots, r$ we have
$$ \text{Ann}_{R/(\pi_1^8, \ldots, \pi_{i - 1}^8)R}(\pi_i) = \text{Ann}_{R/(\pi_1^8, \ldots, \pi_{i - 1}^8)R}(\pi_i^2) $$

and

$$ \text{Ann}_{\Lambda/(\pi_1^8, \ldots, \pi_{i - 1}^8)\Lambda}(\pi_i) = \text{Ann}_{\Lambda/(\pi_1^8, \ldots, \pi_{i - 1}^8)\Lambda}(\pi_i^2) $$
  1. for $i = 1, \ldots, r$ the element $\pi_i$ maps to a strictly standard element in $A$ over $R$.

Then, if

$$ R/(\pi_1^8, \ldots, \pi_r^8)R \to A/(\pi_1^8, \ldots, \pi_r^8)A \to \Lambda/(\pi_1^8, \ldots, \pi_r^8)\Lambda \supset \mathfrak q/(\pi_1^8, \ldots, \pi_r^8)\Lambda $$

can be resolved, so can $R \to A \to \Lambda \supset \mathfrak q$.

Proof. We are going to prove this by induction on $r$.

The case $r = 1$. Here the assumption is that there exists a factorization $A/\pi_1^8 \to \bar C \to \Lambda/\pi_1^8$ which resolves the situation modulo $\pi_1^8$. Conditions (1) and (2) are the assumptions needed to apply Lemma D.22. Thus we can ``lift'' the resolution $\bar C$ to a resolution of $R \to A \to \Lambda \supset \mathfrak q$.

The case $r > 1$. In this case we apply the induction hypothesis for $r - 1$ to the situation $R/\pi_1^8 \to A/\pi_1^8 \to \Lambda/\pi_1^8 \supset \mathfrak q/\pi_1^8\Lambda$. Note that property (2) is preserved by Lemma D.7. The induction resolves the situation modulo $\pi_1^8$; the already proved case $r=1$, applied to $\pi_1$, lifts this resolution to the original situation. ∎

Lemma D.29: delocalize weak

Adapted from the Stacks project, smoothing.tex, lines 2147–2227.

Let $R \to A \to \Lambda \supset \mathfrak q$ be as in Situation D.27. Let $\mathfrak p = R \cap \mathfrak q$. Assume that $\mathfrak q$ is minimal over $\mathfrak h_A$ and that $R_\mathfrak p \to A_\mathfrak p \to \Lambda_\mathfrak q \supset \mathfrak q\Lambda_\mathfrak q$ can be resolved. Then there exists a factorization $A \to C \to \Lambda$ with $C$ of finite presentation such that $H_{C/R} \Lambda \not \subset \mathfrak q$.

Proof. In the assumed resolution of the localized problem, the singular radical of the intermediate algebra is outside the maximal ideal of $\Lambda_{\mathfrak q}$. Its extended singular ideal is therefore the unit ideal: if that ideal were contained in the maximal prime, its radical would be contained there too. D.8 replaces the intermediate algebra by a smooth one, and D.12 gives a standard smooth factorization, both compatible with the prescribed map from $A$ to $\Lambda_{\mathfrak q}$.

Write $A=R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/(g_1,\ldots,g_t)$, with $x_i\mapsto\lambda_i\in\Lambda$. The identity-block construction D.14 includes this prescribed generator list in a presentation of the standard smooth intermediate algebra: $$C=R_{\mathfrak p}[x_1,\ldots,x_n,u_1,\ldots,u_m]/(f_1,\ldots,f_c),\qquad c\ge n.$$ Its selected $c$-variable Jacobian determinant $\delta$ is a unit. The construction adjoins a separate equation for each member of the list, so repeated generator images cause no difficulty. Multiply each $f_j$ by a denominator in $R\setminus\mathfrak p$ to make its coefficients lie in $R$. These factors are units over $R_{\mathfrak p}$, and multiply $\delta$ by their product, so it remains a unit. Put $P=R[x,u]$.

Choose a polynomial representative of $\delta^{-1}$ and of its identity with $\delta$ modulo the equations over $R_{\mathfrak p}$. Clear the finitely many coefficient denominators in that identity; equality of fractions supplies one further element outside $\mathfrak p$ annihilating its error. Their product gives $s_0\notin\mathfrak p$ for which $\delta$ is a unit in $P_{s_0}/(f_j)$. For each $g_i$, its class vanishes in $(P/(f_j))_{\mathfrak p}$, so a localization witness $s_i\notin\mathfrak p$ gives $s_ig_i\in(f_j)$ in $P$. With $s=s_0\prod_i s_i$, the algebra $$C_s=P_s/(f_j)$$ is standard smooth over $R_s$, all $g_i$ vanish there, and it is smooth over $R$ by principal localization and smooth composition. No assertion that $\delta$ fails to be a unit before this localization is needed.

Choose a common denominator $h\in\Lambda\setminus\mathfrak q$ and numerators $\nu_\ell\in\Lambda$ representing the target images of the finitely many $u_\ell$ as $\nu_\ell/h$. For an empty list take $h=1$. Homogenize only these variables: for sufficiently large integers $d_j\ge0$, put $$F_j(x,U,v)=v^{d_j}f_j(x,U/v)\in R[x,U,v].$$ Every $F_j(\lambda,\nu,h)$ is zero in $\Lambda_{\mathfrak q}$. The product of their finite localization annihilator witnesses gives $\lambda_0\notin\mathfrak q$ killing every one of them in $\Lambda$.

Set $$B=R[w,x_1,\ldots,x_n,U_1,\ldots,U_m,v]/(g_i(x),\ wF_j(x,U,v)).$$ Map it to $\Lambda$ by $w\mapsto\lambda_0$, $x_i\mapsto\lambda_i$, $U_\ell\mapsto\nu_\ell$, $v\mapsto h$. Every equation vanishes exactly in $\Lambda$, and the $g_i$ relations give the desired factorization through $A$. Let $b=wvs\in B$. Its image is outside $\mathfrak q$, because each of its three factors is outside that prime.

In $B_b$ the factors $w,v,s$ are units. Substitute $u_\ell=U_\ell/v$, with inverse $U_\ell=vu_\ell$. Each equation $wF_j=0$ becomes $f_j=0$, since $wv^{d_j}$ is a unit. The equations $g_i=0$ are already consequences of those equations in $P_s$. These substitutions give inverse $R$-algebra maps and the exact isomorphism $$B_b\cong C_s[w,w^{-1},v,v^{-1}].$$ This is smooth over $R$ by polynomial extension, principal localization and F.29. Hence $b\in H_{B/R}$, by D.1 and F.67. Since its image is outside $\mathfrak q$, $H_{B/R}\Lambda\not\subset\mathfrak q$. The displayed finite generator and equation lists make $B$ finitely presented, proving the lemma without adding any Noetherian hypothesis on the target. ∎

Lemma D.30: delocalize height zero

Adapted from the Stacks project, smoothing.tex, lines 2229–2274.

Let $R \to A \to \Lambda \supset \mathfrak q$ be as in Situation D.27. Let $\mathfrak p = R \cap \mathfrak q$. Assume

  1. $\mathfrak q$ is minimal over $\mathfrak h_A$,

  2. $R_\mathfrak p \to A_\mathfrak p \to \Lambda_\mathfrak q \supset \mathfrak q\Lambda_\mathfrak q$ can be resolved, and

  3. $\dim(\Lambda_\mathfrak q) = 0$.

Then $R \to A \to \Lambda \supset \mathfrak q$ can be resolved.

Proof. The Noetherian hypothesis is on $R$; no Noetherian hypothesis on $\Lambda$ is needed. By AG-CA-03, Theorem 2.1, the finite type $R$-algebra $A$ is Noetherian. Choose $H_{A/R}=(a_1,\ldots,a_r)$.

A zero-dimensional local ring has only its maximal prime: a strictly smaller prime would give a chain of length one. Thus the nilradical of $\Lambda_{\mathfrak q}$ is $\mathfrak q\Lambda_{\mathfrak q}$, by the prime-intersection argument in D.5. Since $\mathfrak q$ contains $\mathfrak h_A$, every $a_i$ has nilpotent image in this localization. Choose one positive exponent $N$ killing their finite list. The definition of localization gives $\lambda_i\notin\mathfrak q$ with $\lambda_i a_i^N=0$ in $\Lambda$. Their product $\lambda\notin\mathfrak q$ satisfies $$\lambda a_i^N=0\qquad(1\le i\le r).$$ For an empty list choose $N=1$ and $\lambda=1$. This uses only these finitely many nilpotence witnesses; it does not assert that the local ring is Artinian or that its entire maximal ideal is nilpotent.

Apply D.29 to the assumed localized resolution. It gives $A\to C\to\Lambda$, with $C$ finitely presented over $R$ and $\mathfrak h_C\not\subset\mathfrak q$. There is a finite $A$-presentation $C=A[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/(f_1,\ldots,f_m)$: adjoining the generators of a finite $R$-presentation makes it a finite type $A$-algebra, and the polynomial ring over the Noetherian $A$ has finite ideal kernels by the same Hilbert theorem. Choose $c\in H_{C/R}$ whose image is outside $\mathfrak q$. Such an element exists, since otherwise the radical of $H_{C/R}\Lambda$ would be contained in this prime.

Define $$B=A[x_1,\ldots,x_n,y_1,\ldots,y_r,z,t_{ij}]/ \left(f_j-\sum_{i=1}^r y_i t_{ij},\ zy_i\right),$$ with $1\le j\le m$. This is finitely presented over $R$. It maps to $\Lambda$ by the given map on $C$, by $x_i$ going to the corresponding generator image, by $y_i\mapsto a_i^N$, $z\mapsto\lambda$ and $t_{ij}\mapsto0$. The displayed annihilator equality makes every equation $zy_i$ vanish, and the other equations reduce to $f_j=0$.

Inverting $z$ forces every $y_i=0$, giving the exact elimination $$B_z\cong C[z,z^{-1},t_{ij}].$$ Consequently $B_{zc}$ is smooth over $R$. Here and below a principal open lying in the smooth locus is globally smooth by F.67. For each $\ell$, inverting $y_\ell$ instead forces $z=0$ and solves every equation uniquely for $t_{\ell j}$: $$t_{\ell j}=y_\ell^{-1}\left(f_j-\sum_{i\ne\ell}y_i t_{ij}\right).$$ Hence $$B_{y_\ell}\cong A[x_j,y_i,y_\ell^{-1},t_{ij}\ (i\ne\ell)],$$ a polynomial extension and principal localization over $A$. Since $A_{a_\ell}$ is smooth over $R$, $B_{a_\ell y_\ell}$ is smooth over $R$ as well. Thus $zc$ and all $a_\ell y_\ell$ belong to $H_{B/R}$.

The image of $zc$ in $\Lambda$ is $\lambda c\notin\mathfrak q$, so $\mathfrak h_B\not\subset\mathfrak q$. The image of $a_\ell y_\ell$ is $a_\ell^{N+1}$, so each image $a_\ell$ belongs to the radical $\mathfrak h_B$. Taking radicals gives $\mathfrak h_A\subset\mathfrak h_B$. The finite presentation and the two required radical conditions prove that $A\to B\to\Lambda$ is the desired resolution. ∎

Separable residue fields

In this section we explain how to solve a local problem in the case of a separable residue field extension.

Lemma D.31: ogoma

Adapted from the Stacks project, smoothing.tex, lines 2286–2303.

Let $A$ be a Noetherian ring and let $M$ be a finite $A$-module. Let $S \subset A$ be a multiplicative set. If $\pi \in A$ and $\ker(\pi : S^{-1}M \to S^{-1}M) = \ker(\pi^2 : S^{-1}M \to S^{-1}M)$ then there exists an $s \in S$ such that for any $n > 0$ we have $\ker(s^n\pi : M \to M) = \ker((s^n\pi)^2 : M \to M)$.

Proof. Let $K = \ker(\pi : M \to M)$ and $K' = \{m \in M \mid \pi^2 m = 0\text{ in }S^{-1}M\}$ and $Q = K'/K$. Note that $S^{-1}Q = 0$ by assumption. Since $A$ is Noetherian we see that $Q$ is a finite $A$-module. Hence we can find an $s \in S$ such that $s$ annihilates $Q$. If $(s^n\pi)^2m=0$, then $\pi^2m=0$ after localization, so $m\in K'$. The equality $sQ=0$ gives $sm\in K$, hence $s\pi m=0$, and therefore $s^n\pi m=0$ for every $n>0$. The reverse kernel inclusion is immediate. Thus this single $s$ works for every positive power. ∎

Lemma D.32: find sequence

Adapted from the Stacks project, smoothing.tex, lines 2305–2349.

Let $\Lambda$ be a Noetherian ring. Let $I \subset \Lambda$ be an ideal. Let $I \subset \mathfrak q$ be a prime. Let $n, e$ be positive integers. Assume that $\mathfrak q^n\Lambda_\mathfrak q \subset I\Lambda_\mathfrak q$ and that $\Lambda_\mathfrak q$ is a regular local ring of dimension $d$. Then there exist $\pi_1, \ldots, \pi_d \in \Lambda$ such that

  1. $(\pi_1, \ldots, \pi_d)\Lambda_\mathfrak q = \mathfrak q\Lambda_\mathfrak q$,

  2. $\pi_1^n, \ldots, \pi_d^n \in I$, and

  3. for $i = 1, \ldots, d$ we have

$$ \text{Ann}_{\Lambda/(\pi_1^e, \ldots, \pi_{i - 1}^e)\Lambda}(\pi_i) = \text{Ann}_{\Lambda/(\pi_1^e, \ldots, \pi_{i - 1}^e)\Lambda}(\pi_i^2). $$

Proof. Set $S = \Lambda \setminus \mathfrak q$ so that $\Lambda_\mathfrak q = S^{-1}\Lambda$. First pick $\pi_1, \ldots, \pi_d$ with (1) which is possible as $\Lambda_\mathfrak q$ is regular. By assumption $\pi_i^n \in I\Lambda_\mathfrak q$. Thus we can find $s_1, \ldots, s_d \in S$ such that $s_i\pi_i^n \in I$. Replacing $\pi_i$ by $s_i\pi_i$ we get (2). Note that (1) and (2) are preserved by further multiplying by elements of $S$. Suppose that (3) holds for $i = 1, \ldots, t$ for some $t \in \{0, \ldots, d\}$. Note that $\pi_1, \ldots, \pi_d$ is a regular sequence in $S^{-1}\Lambda$, see Algebra, Lemma AG-CA-12, Theorem 6.1. In particular $\pi_1^e, \ldots, \pi_t^e, \pi_{t + 1}$ is a regular sequence in $S^{-1}\Lambda = \Lambda_\mathfrak q$ by Algebra, Lemma AG-CA-12, Proposition 1.3. Hence we see that

$$ \text{Ann}_{S^{-1}\Lambda/(\pi_1^e, \ldots, \pi_{i - 1}^e)}(\pi_i) = \text{Ann}_{S^{-1}\Lambda/(\pi_1^e, \ldots, \pi_{i - 1}^e)}(\pi_i^2). $$

Thus we get (3) for $i = t + 1$ after replacing $\pi_{t + 1}$ by $s\pi_{t + 1}$ for some $s \in S$ by Lemma D.31. By induction on $t$ this produces a sequence satisfying (1), (2), and (3). ∎

Lemma D.33: resolve special

Adapted from the Stacks project, smoothing.tex, lines 2351–2430.

Let $k \to A \to \Lambda \supset \mathfrak q$ be as in Situation D.27 where

  1. $k$ is a field,

  2. $\Lambda$ is Noetherian,

  3. $\mathfrak q$ is minimal over $\mathfrak h_A$,

  4. $\Lambda_\mathfrak q$ is a regular local ring, and

  5. the field extension $\kappa(\mathfrak q)/k$ is separable.

Then $k \to A \to \Lambda \supset \mathfrak q$ can be resolved.

Proof. Put $L=\Lambda_{\mathfrak q}$ and $d=\dim L$. If $d=0$, regularity makes $L$ its residue field: its zero cotangent dimension and finite-module Nakayama give zero maximal ideal. By the separability hypothesis, F.23 writes $L$ as a filtered colimit of smooth $k$-algebras. Since $A$ is finitely presented, F.90 gives a smooth factorization of $A\to L$. Its singular ideal is the unit ideal, so it resolves the localized problem. D.30 gives the required original resolution. Assume $d>0$.

Set $I=H_{A/k}\Lambda$. Minimality of $\mathfrak q$ gives $\sqrt{IL}=\mathfrak qL$. The maximal ideal of the Noetherian local ring $L$ has a finite generating list, with a power of each generator in $IL$. Every monomial of degree greater than the sum of those powers minus one contains the required power of some generator. Thus choose $n>0$ with $\mathfrak q^nL\subset IL$. The algebra $A$ is Noetherian by AG-CA-03, Theorem 2.1, so choose $H_{A/k}=(a_1,\ldots,a_r)$.

Put $R=k[x_1,\ldots,x_d]$ and $$B=A[x_1,\ldots,x_d,z_{ij}]/\left(x_i^n-\sum_{j=1}^r z_{ij}a_j\right).$$ On inverting $a_j$, the $i$th equation solves uniquely for $z_{ij}$. Therefore $B_{a_j}$ is a polynomial algebra over $A_{a_j}[x_1,\ldots,x_d]$, smooth over $R$ by base change and polynomial extension. In $B_{x_i}$ the elements $a_j$ generate the unit ideal, since $1=x_i^{-n}\sum_jz_{ij}a_j$. Their principal charts cover its spectrum, so F.67 makes $B_{x_i}$ smooth over $R$.

Use D.9 to construct $B\to C=\operatorname{Sym}_B(M)$ with retraction $C\to B$, where $M$ is the conormal of a finite presentation of $B$. Its smooth-case proof makes $M_{x_i}$ finite projective and $C_{x_i}$ smooth over $B_{x_i}$, and identifies $\Omega_{C_{x_i}/R}$ as finite free. Thus $C_{x_i}$ is smooth over $R$ with free differentials. The finite type algebra $C$ is finitely presented over the Noetherian $R$: a finite polynomial surjection has a finite ideal kernel by the Hilbert theorem. Part (e) of D.15 supplies a threshold for each $x_i$; choose one common positive $c$ at least all these thresholds. Every $x_i^c$ is strictly standard in $C/R$. This uses the proved strictly-standard implication, not the disproved original elementary-power implication.

Apply D.32 to $I\subset\Lambda$, with this fixed $n$ and $e=8c$. It gives $\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_d$ generating the maximal ideal of $L$, satisfying $\pi_i^n\in I$ in $\Lambda$ and the required annihilator equalities modulo previous $e$th powers. Write $\pi_i^n=\sum_ja_j\lambda_{ij}$ in $\Lambda$. The assignments $x_i\mapsto\pi_i$, $z_{ij}\mapsto\lambda_{ij}$ define $B\to\Lambda$. Compose with the retraction to get $C\to\Lambda$; together with $R\to\Lambda$ these give the required commuting maps from $A$.

We may pass from the original problem to $R\to C\to\Lambda$. Indeed $B_{a_j}$ and $C_{a_j}$ are smooth over $R$, so the images of $a_j$ belong to $H_{C/R}$. A resolution $C\to T\to\Lambda$ therefore has $\mathfrak h_A\subset\mathfrak h_{T/R}$. Since $R$ is a polynomial algebra over $k$, smoothness over $R$ implies smoothness over $k$ by composition. Thus $H_{T/R}\subset H_{T/k}$. Also $T$ is finitely presented over $k$, by appending its finite equations to those for the polynomial base. This gives both radical conditions for an original resolution over $k$.

Apply D.28 to $x_1^c,\ldots,x_d^c$. Its strictly-standard condition was established above. In $R/(x_1^e,\ldots,x_{i-1}^e)$ multiplication by the remaining polynomial variable $x_i$ is injective, by comparison of polynomial coefficients. Hence both relevant annihilators are zero. On the target quotient, D.32 gives $\ker(\pi_i)=\ker(\pi_i^2)$. This implies $\ker(\pi_i^r)=\ker(\pi_i)$ for every $r\ge1$: inductively, $\pi_i^{r+1}v=0$ puts $\pi_i^{r-1}v$ in $\ker(\pi_i^2)=\ker(\pi_i)$, so $\pi_i^rv=0$. In particular the kernels for $\pi_i^c$ and $\pi_i^{2c}$ agree. These are exactly the target hypotheses of D.28, since $(x_i^c)^8=x_i^e$ and likewise for $\pi_i$.

It remains to resolve the quotient problem over $R_0=R/(x_1^e,\ldots,x_d^e)$. After localization at the target prime its base is $$S=R_{(x_1,\ldots,x_d)}/(x_1^e,\ldots,x_d^e),$$ and its target is $L_0=L/(\pi_1^e,\ldots,\pi_d^e)$. The contraction to $R$ is exactly $(x_1,\ldots,x_d)$, since a polynomial has residue its constant in the field $k$. The prequotient base $R_{(x_1,\ldots,x_d)}$ is regular local with parameters $x_1,\ldots,x_d$. Their images $\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_d$ form a regular sequence in the regular local ring $L$, by AG-CA-12, Proposition 1.3. F.46 gives flatness before quotienting, and base change gives flatness of $S\to L_0$.

The maximal ideal of $S$ is nilpotent, by the same bounded-degree monomial calculation. Its residue field is $k$, and $L_0$ modulo that ideal is $\kappa(\mathfrak q)$, a separable extension of $k$. By F.23 this residue field is a smooth colimit; D.18, applied to the nilpotent maximal ideal of $S$ and the flat target, makes $L_0$ a filtered colimit of smooth $S$-algebras. F.90 therefore factors the finitely presented localized algebra $C\otimes_R S$ through a smooth $S$-algebra.

Finally $L_0$ is zero dimensional. Its maximal ideal is generated by the $\pi_i$, and any sufficiently high-degree monomial contains a $\pi_i^e$, so this ideal is nilpotent. If the singular radical of the quotient input is already outside the target prime, the identity factorization resolves that quotient. Otherwise the target prime is minimal over it, since its localization has dimension zero. D.30 delocalizes the smooth factorization just constructed. D.28 then lifts that resolution to $R\to C\to\Lambda$, and the preceding change-of-base argument returns it to $k\to A\to\Lambda$. ∎

Inseparable residue fields

In this section we explain how to solve a local problem in the case of an inseparable residue field extension.

Lemma D.34: helper

Adapted from the Stacks project, smoothing.tex, lines 2444–2549.

Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p > 0$. Let $(\Lambda, \mathfrak m, K)$ be an Artinian local $k$-algebra. Assume that $\dim H_1(L_{K/k}) < \infty$. Then $\Lambda$ is a filtered colimit of Artinian local $k$-algebras $A$ with each map $A \to \Lambda$ flat, with $\mathfrak m_A \Lambda = \mathfrak m$, and with $A$ essentially of finite type over $k$.

Proof. Write $i\colon k\to\Lambda$ for the specified structure map and identify $k$ with its image in the residue field $K$. The Artinian-local theorem AG-CA-03, Theorem 4.2, gives a finite generating list $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d$ of $\mathfrak m$ and an integer $n\ge1$ with $\mathfrak m^n=0$.

Every field is formally smooth over its prime field, by the complete arbitrary-field lifting proof AG-CA-19S, Lemma 1.1, recalled in F.91. Square-zero lifting extends to a nilpotent ideal by successively lifting through its powers: the kernel of $E/J^{a+1}\to E/J^a$ is square zero for $a\ge1$. Thus there is a coefficient-field section $\sigma\colon K\to\Lambda$. This need not agree with $i$ on $k$. For any such section define $\Psi_\sigma\colon K[x_1,\ldots,x_d]\to\Lambda$ by $x_j\mapsto\lambda_j$.

We first arrange a section $\sigma$ and a finitely generated intermediate field $k\subset F_0\subset K$ such that $$i(k)\subset\Psi_\sigma(F_0[x_1,\ldots,x_d]).$$ Prove this claim by induction on the least nilpotence exponent. For $n=1$, $\Lambda=K$ and the identity section with $F_0=k$ works. For $n>1$ put $I=\mathfrak m^{n-1}$ and $\Lambda'=\Lambda/I$. Here $I^2=0$ and $\mathfrak m I=0$. The preceding claim supplies a section $\sigma'\colon K\to\Lambda'$ and a finitely generated field $F'\supset k$ containing the prescribed $k$-map in the subring generated by $\sigma'(F')$ and the images of the $\lambda_j$. Lift $\sigma'$ to $\sigma$ by formal smoothness.

The truncated polynomial ring $$T=F'[x_1,\ldots,x_d]/(x_1,\ldots,x_d)^n$$ maps to $\Lambda$ by $\Psi_\sigma$ and onto that subring of $\Lambda'$. The latter surjection has nilpotent kernel: its kernel has zero constant coefficient, since $F'\hookrightarrow K$, and lies in the nilpotent ideal $(x_j)$. Formal smoothness of $k/\mathbb F_p$ lifts the prescribed $k$-map to a ring map $\tau\colon k\to T$. The maps $i$ and $\Psi_\sigma\tau$ agree modulo $I$. Their difference $\theta\colon k\to I$ is an $\mathbb F_p$-derivation, with scalar action through $k\subset K$, by expansion of products and $I^2=0$.

The absolute p-basis theorem F.119 gives a basis $dy_j$ of $\Omega_{k/\mathbb F_p}$ consisting of differentials of field elements. Formal smoothness and F.17 give $H_1(L_{K/\mathbb F_p})=0$. The exact field sequence F.131 therefore gives $$0\longrightarrow H_1(L_{K/k})\longrightarrow\Omega_{k/\mathbb F_p}\otimes_kK\longrightarrow\Omega_{K/\mathbb F_p}\longrightarrow\Omega_{K/k}\longrightarrow0.$$ Its finite-dimensional first image has a finite basis, each vector of which has finite support in the $dy_j$. Choose the union $J_0$ of these supports. The images of $dy_j$ for $j\notin J_0$ are independent: a relation supported outside $J_0$ would lie in a subspace supported inside $J_0$, so it is zero. Prescribe a $K$-linear map on their span with value $\theta(y_j)$, extend a basis to the whole differential space, and give the added basis vectors value zero in the $K$-vector space $I$. The universal derivation gives $D\colon K\to I$ with $D(y_j)=\theta(y_j)$ for $j\notin J_0$.

Replace $\sigma$ by $\sigma+D$. The derivation identity and $I^2=0$ show directly that this is a ring map, and it remains a residue section. The change in $\Psi_\sigma\tau(a)$ is exactly $D(a)$: the constant coefficient of $\tau(a)$ has residue $a$, while a change $D(c)$ in any positive-degree coefficient is killed by its monomial in $\mathfrak m$, because $\mathfrak m I=0$. Thus the new error is $\theta-D|_k$. If $da=\sum_j a_jdy_j$, it equals $$\sum_{j\in J_0}a_jf_j,\qquad f_j=(\theta-D|_k)(y_j)\in I.$$ Since $I=\mathfrak m^{n-1}$ and $\mathfrak m I=0$, every $f_j$ is a combination of the finitely many degree-$(n-1)$ monomials $\lambda^E$, with coefficients from $K$ through the section. Adjoin these finitely many coefficients to $F'$, giving $F_0$. The coefficients $a_j$ above belong to $k\subset F_0$, and $\tau(a)$ has coefficients in $F'$. Hence both $\Psi_\sigma\tau(a)$ and its correction lie in $\Psi_\sigma(F_0[x])$. This proves the claim for the actual map $i$, rather than only its residue map.

Fix this section. The map $\Psi_\sigma$ is surjective. Indeed, subtract the coefficient-field representative of an element's residue, express the remainder using the $\lambda_j$, and repeat on the coefficients of that remainder. At degree $n$ the remainder vanishes, giving a finite polynomial expression. Its kernel is generated by finitely many polynomials $g_1,\ldots,g_t$ by the Hilbert basis theorem AG-CA-03, Theorem 2.1. Adjoin all their coefficients to $F_0$ and call the resulting finitely generated field $F_*$. For every finitely generated intermediate field $F\supset F_*$ put $$A_F=F[x_1,\ldots,x_d]/(g_1,\ldots,g_t).$$ Tensoring the displayed presentation gives the exact identity $K\otimes_F A_F=\Lambda$. A basis of $K/F$ containing $1$ identifies this tensor product, as an $A_F$-module, with a direct sum of copies of $A_F$. The $1$-coordinate proves that $A_F\to\Lambda$ is injective; the same basis proves faithful flatness. The earlier claim makes its image a $k$-subalgebra for the specified map $i$.

The ideal $(x_1,\ldots,x_d)$ of $A_F$ has $n$th power zero, by the injection into $\Lambda$. Its quotient is $F$, since every kernel polynomial has zero constant coefficient. Thus $A_F$ is spanned over $F$ by the finitely many monomials of degree below $n$. It is Artinian local with that maximal ideal: an element with nonzero constant coefficient has an inverse by the finite geometric series in its nilpotent part, and finite vector-space dimension makes every ideal chain stabilize. Its maximal ideal extends to $\mathfrak m$, generated by the same $\lambda_j$.

The residue map $k\to F$ is the original subfield inclusion, with $F/k$ finitely generated. It is essentially of finite type, as the fraction field of a finitely generated $k$-domain. F.40 therefore makes $A_F$ essentially of finite type over $k$, even though its coefficient-field inclusion need not be the structure map.

Finally these embedded algebras form a directed family: the field generated by two finite field-generator lists is a common successor. Every element of $\Lambda$ has the finite polynomial expression established above; adjoining its finitely many coefficients to $F_*$ puts it in one $A_F$. Their union, hence their filtered colimit, is exactly $\Lambda$. All transition maps are the actual inclusions, and every member has every asserted property. ∎

Lemma D.34A: Artinian denominator enlargement

Let $k$ have characteristic $p>0$. Let $A\to B$ be a flat local map of Noetherian Artinian local $k$-algebras, with $\mathfrak m_AB=\mathfrak m_B$, and suppose $\mathfrak m_B^n=0$. Write $F$ and $K$ for their residue fields. For finitely many units $b_j\in B$, there is a factorization $A\to A'\to B$ by local maps such that $A\to A'$ is essentially smooth, $A'\to B$ is faithfully flat, $\mathfrak m_{A'}B=\mathfrak m_B$, and a $p$-power of each $b_j$ belongs to $A'$. If a residue $\bar b_j$ is transcendental over the current residue field, the construction adjoins $b_j$ itself. The residue extension $F'/F$ is a finite tower of simple transcendental and finite separable extensions.

Proof. Treat one unit $b$ at a time. If its residue $\beta$ is transcendental over $F$, use $A'=A[T]_{\mathfrak m_AA[T]}$ with $T\mapsto b$. Its residue field is $F(\beta)$: every nonzero polynomial in $F[T]$ is inverted. Each inverted element maps to a unit of $B$, so the map is defined and local. This localization is essentially smooth, with $\mathfrak m_{A'}=\mathfrak m_AA'$. It is Noetherian by the Hilbert basis theorem and localization, and this maximal ideal is nilpotent. Its successive ideal-power quotients are finite-dimensional over $F(\beta)$, because each ideal power is finite in the Noetherian ring. They give a finite composition series; thus the ring is Artinian. This argument also proves Artinity of the finite free algebra in the algebraic case below.

If $\beta$ is algebraic over $F$, choose a $p$-power $q_0$ for which $\beta^{q_0}$ is separable over $F$, by the inseparable exponent calculation already proved. Lift the monic separable minimal polynomial of $\beta^{q_0}$ from $F[T]$ to $h\in A[T]$ and put $A'=A[T]/(h)$. It is finite free over $A$. Its quotient modulo $\mathfrak m_A$ is the field $F(\beta^{q_0})$, and $\mathfrak m_AA'$ is nilpotent, so $A'$ is Artinian local with this maximal ideal. Bézout for the relatively prime residue polynomials $\bar h,\bar h'$ makes $h'$ a unit modulo $\mathfrak m_AA'$; lifting its inverse across a nilpotent ideal makes it a unit in $A'$. The square Jacobian calculation, AG-CA-17, Theorem 4.1 and Section 6, therefore makes $A'$ étale. The simple-root Hensel proof in AG-CA-19, Theorem 5.1, lifts the specified residue root in the Artinian local ring $B$ and gives $A'\to B$. This is exactly the finite étale lifting construction in F.54, written here in its consumed form. If $\beta\in F$, use instead $A'=A$, $q_0=1$.

In both cases $A'$ is flat over $A$, and $A'/\mathfrak m_AA'=F'$, its residue field. A free $A$-resolution of $F$ therefore becomes a free $A'$-resolution of $F'$ after tensoring. Tensor it further with $B$. Flatness of $B$ over $A$ gives

$$ \operatorname{Tor}^{A'}_1(F',B)=\operatorname{Tor}^{A}_1(F,B)=0. $$

The Noetherian local criterion, AG-CA-08, Theorem 4.2, applied with finite $B$-module $B$, proves that $A'\to B$ is flat. It is local and hence faithfully flat, so in particular injective. Its maximal ideal still generates $\mathfrak m_B$.

In the algebraic case choose $x\in A'$ with residue $\beta^{-q_0}$. It is a unit. Then $xb^{q_0}-1\in\mathfrak m_B$. For a $p$-power $q_1\ge n$, Frobenius gives $(xb^{q_0})^{q_1}=1$, whence $b^{q_0q_1}=x^{-q_1}\in A'$. In the transcendental case $b$ is already present, so any $p$-power may be used. Repeating the finite construction proves every assertion.

We also record its differential effect, used immediately below. For a simple transcendental residue extension the polynomial presentation and localization give $\Omega_{F(\beta)/k}=(\Omega_{F/k}\otimes_FF(\beta))\oplus F(\beta)\,d\beta$. A finite separable residue extension gives the same old differential space after tensoring: its monic separable presentation has invertible derivative, so its relative conormal complex is acyclic. The field Jacobi–Zariski sequence F.131 likewise gives in both cases

$$ H_1(L_{F'/k})=H_1(L_{F/k})\otimes_FF'. $$

These are natural identifications, and composition gives them for the finite tower. Thus the image of this first homology in $H_1(L_{K/k})$ is unchanged. ∎

Lemma D.35: solution modulo

Adapted from the Stacks project, smoothing.tex, lines 2551–2621.

Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p > 0$. Let $\Lambda$ be a Noetherian geometrically regular $k$-algebra. Let $\mathfrak q \subset \Lambda$ be a prime ideal.
